options.text: It rescales a benefit measured over one horizon onto a common basis, so a longer horizon scores lower
It converts the assessed saving into cash in the year of installation, so every horizon is valued alike
options.misconception: believes the factor removes all timing differences

options.text: It measures the fraction of the saving that survives after the assessor takes a service fee
options.misconception: treats the factor as a share paid to the assessor

options.misconception: reads the factor as a payback period in years

questions.explanation: An equivalence factor puts benefits measured over different time horizons onto one comparable basis. A shorter horizon therefore attracts a larger factor than a longer one.
questions.hint: Ask what the factor does to the benefit before comparison.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A denominator that makes the indicator improve
questions.learningObjective: Design a check on an indicator whose denominator may have moved
questions.stem: A screening programme is judged by the proportion of cases found among those screened. Design a check that would show whether a fall in the rate reflects a real improvement rather than a change in who was screened.

answer.exemplar: Record the number of people screened and the number of cases detected in each period along with the screening criteria and the referral routes, then recompute the rate on a fixed case definition with the same age and risk bands. If the rate falls when the mix of people screened is held constant, the improvement is real; if it falls only because screening shifted towards lower-risk groups, the headline change is an artefact of who was included rather than of better health outcomes.

questions.explanation: The check must hold the population screened constant while the outcome is recomputed, or the rate moves with the denominator rather than with health. Referral routes show whether case finding changed.
questions.hint: Recompute the rate on a fixed case mix.

questions.stem: A recycling note records that paper collected from 12,400 households was reprocessed at 8,050 tonnes against 10,200 tonnes collected. Explain what this tells a clinician advising households about waste.

answer.exemplar: The note shows that roughly 79 percent of collected paper was reprocessed, with the balance diverted elsewhere, most likely to landfill or to energy recovery, which is not the same as recycling. For the clinic's purposes the figure is the diversion rate for one material only, and it says nothing about how much the households themselves recycled or about the other materials in their bins. Advising residents on that single number without that context risks implying a level of circularity the scheme has not achieved.

questions.explanation: The note gives a rate for one material and one collection round. The unreprocessed fifth is diverted rather than recycled.
questions.hint: Ask what the unprocessed fifth of the tonnage became.

questions.topic: A fixed charge after the sector consolidates
questions.learningObjective: Design a study of a consolidated fixed charge by consumption band
questions.stem: Design a study that would show whether a higher fixed charge after tariff consolidation actually raises the cost for low-use households in a clinic's advice area.

answer.exemplar: Compare bills for a matched set of households either side of the consolidation date, grouping them by annual consumption bands and income band, then compute the fixed element as a share of each bill before and after. Households in the lowest consumption band will show the largest proportional increase if the fixed charge is doing what is claimed, so the analysis must report that group separately rather than an average across all households, and must state how many households sit in each band.

questions.explanation: The design must separate consumption from income and report the lowest band on its own. Sample sizes per band must be reported alongside results.
questions.hint: Stratify by consumption band and report the lowest band.

questions.topic: What a single permit leaves unexamined
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of a single site-wide permit
questions.stem: A clinic file notes that a single discharge permit for a small industrial site covers four separate outlets across two years of operation. Explain what such a permit leaves unexamined.

answer.exemplar: A single permit fixes a limit for the whole site and does not reveal how the limit is used in practice at each outlet, in which season, or under which operating conditions. It therefore cannot show whether one stream is dominating the load, whether flows have changed since the permit was issued, or whether the monitoring requirements are matched to the actual risk. The clinic's advice on respiratory exposure needs outlet-level and time-resolved data that the permit itself does not generate.

questions.explanation: A site-wide limit hides how the discharge is actually split between outlets and seasons. Advice on exposure needs outlet-level and time-resolved data that a single aggregate permit does not produce.
questions.hint: Ask how discharge is split across outlets.

questions.topic: A price rise that does not lose revenue
questions.learningObjective: Design a study separating price and volume effects on revenue
questions.stem: Propose a study that would establish whether a clinic's service price rise raised or cut its total revenue.

answer.exemplar: Record the price actually charged and the number of services delivered for each period, then compute revenue as price times volume and compare it with the same product for the period before the change. Because volume may respond to price, the design should hold capacity and staffing constant where possible, or use a comparable clinic that did not change price as a control, and should report how much of the revenue change comes from price and how much from volume rather than treating the two as one number.

questions.explanation: Revenue must be decomposed into price and volume so the two effects are not confused. Reporting the split is what makes the result interpretable.
questions.hint: Split revenue into price and volume effects.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Equivalence factors that depend on the horizon
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the same saving earns a lower credit on a longer horizon
questions.stem: A clinic note explains that a patient's insulation saving is credited at 0.92 over twenty years but 0.61 over fifty. Explain why the same saving receives a lower credit on the longer horizon.

answer.exemplar: Equivalence factors exist so that schemes measured over different horizons can be compared on one basis, and the factor records how much of a benefit survives when it is stretched further into the future. Extending a horizon discounts more of the benefit, because money and comfort arriving later are worth less to the household and the climate effect is assumed to decay as the equipment ages and is replaced. The lower factor on the fifty-year case therefore reflects a real reduction in credited value, not a change in the physical saving.

questions.explanation: A longer horizon stretches the benefit further into the future, where it is worth less and decays more. The physical saving is unchanged; what changes is how much of it is credited for comparison.
questions.hint: Think about a benefit stretched over more years.

questions.topic: A fixed price as a share of a falling income
questions.learningObjective: Design a study measuring the fixed element of a household bill
questions.stem: Set out a study that would measure how much of a household's energy bill is a fixed price that does not change when it uses less.

answer.exemplar: Recruit households across a wide range of consumption, record half-hourly or daily meter readings alongside their bills and tariff statements, and then regress the billed amount on measured consumption to estimate the intercept. That intercept is the fixed component of the bill, and it can be expressed as a share of each household's income to show how the burden falls on low users. Seasonal patterns, standing charges and any block tariff must be handled in the design, since a mis-specified tariff would bias the estimate of the fixed element.

questions.explanation: Measuring consumption and billing together lets the fixed element be estimated as the intercept rather than assumed from the tariff sheet. Income must also be recorded so it reads as a burden.
questions.hint: Regress billed amount on measured consumption.

questions.topic: Sharing auction revenue between households
questions.learningObjective: Explain the distributional effect of equal and pro-rata shares
questions.stem: A note on an energy auction records that revenue is shared among 850 households in equal shares, with a separate rebate paid to those with high bills. Explain what this does and does not achieve.

answer.exemplar: The equal share spreads a fixed pot across the community, which is simple to administer and easy to explain, but it gives a low-income household with a small bill the same amount as a household with a large one, so it is weakly targeted on need. The separate rebate restores some progressivity because it scales with bills, though bills themselves rise with consumption rather than with need. Together the two instruments broaden participation, but neither reaches households with high needs and low bills, and the note should say so plainly.

questions.explanation: An equal split ignores need entirely while a bill-weighted rebate follows consumption rather than hardship. The pair widens participation but still misses households with high needs and low bills.
questions.hint: Compare what each of the two shares actually responds to.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A denominator that makes the indicator improve
questions.learningObjective: Design a recomputation to test an indicator's denominator
questions.stem: Devise a study that would show whether a fall in a clinic's reported complication rate is real or an artefact of the denominator used.

answer.exemplar: Recalculate the complication rate over the same period using a fixed denominator, such as all procedures performed or all patients enrolled at the start of the period, rather than whichever base was used for the headline. Then test whether the revised series still shows the improvement, and record what changed in the denominator, the case definition and the follow-up period between the two reports. A rate that only looks good because fewer, healthier patients were counted in the denominator will not survive recalculation on a fixed base.

questions.explanation: Recomputing on a fixed base removes the denominator effect. The definition and follow-up window must also be held constant or they will substitute for the denominator effect.

answer.exemplar: A single annual sample cannot represent a discharge that varies by season, by shift or by production run, so the permit may characterise an unrepresentative week and set its limits around that figure. questions.learningObjective: Explain the comparison problem equivalence factors solve
questions.stem: One clinic note states that an equivalence factor is applied to a scheme's benefit before schemes over different horizons are ranked. Explain what problem this step is intended to solve.

answer.exemplar: Without a common basis, a scheme delivering a small benefit over five years competes directly against one delivering a large benefit over fifty years, and the short scheme wins on the arithmetic of when its benefits arrive rather than on their size or their durability. Applying horizon-specific factors removes that timing advantage, so that a longer-lived scheme is credited for the longer service it actually provides. It does not settle value or cost, but it stops the comparison being decided by timing alone.

questions.topic: A price rise that does not lose revenue
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a revenue change of less than one percent
questions.stem: The clinic's records show a price of 14 pounds per unit on 4,000 units sold, then 15.50 pounds on 3,600 units. What does this show about the revenue change?

options.text: Revenue falls from 56,000 to 55,800 pounds, so a price rise was nearly offset by lower volume
Revenue rises from 56,000 to 55,800 pounds, so the price rise outweighed the lost volume
options.misconception: reads a near-flat total as a clear gain

options.text: Revenue falls from 56,000 to 55,800 pounds, so the price rise had no effect on the total
options.misconception: treats a near-flat result as no effect

options.text: Revenue falls steeply, so the units figure must be recorded wrongly in the clinic's notes
options.misconception: dismisses the record rather than reading it

questions.explanation: Revenue moves from 56,000 to 55,800 pounds, a fall of about 0.4 percent. The 10.7 percent price rise was almost exactly cancelled by the 10 percent fall in volume, so the total is close to unchanged.
questions.hint: Multiply price by units in each period.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Equivalence factors that depend on the horizon
questions.learningObjective: Compute an adjusted credit across two horizons
questions.stem: A further clinic note records an assessed benefit of 400,000 pounds, split evenly between a twenty-year horizon credited at 0.78 and a fifty-year horizon credited at 0.54. What is the adjusted credit in total, in pounds?
questions.explanation: Half the benefit, 200,000 pounds, is credited at 0.78 to give 156,000 pounds, and the other half at 0.54 gives 108,000 pounds. The adjusted credit is therefore 264,000 pounds.
questions.hint: Apply each factor to its half of the benefit and add.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A fixed charge after the sector consolidates
questions.learningObjective: Design a study of a stand-alone tariff before consolidation
questions.stem: Plan a study that would show how a utility's consolidation into a single fixed charge affected tenants who had been on a stand-alone tariff beforehand.

answer.exemplar: Identify tenants on the old stand-alone tariff and a matched group on the tariff that replaced it, then compare their bills over the same twelve months either side of consolidation, holding occupancy and consumption constant where possible and adjusting for the change in fixed and variable rates separately. The two groups must differ only in the tariff they faced, otherwise the comparison confounds consolidation with the households involved. Reporting both the total bill change and the split between fixed and variable elements shows where the gain or loss falls.

questions.explanation: Matching on occupancy and consumption keeps the comparison to the tariff change. An unmatched comparison would confound consolidation with the households involved.
questions.hint: Match tenants and split fixed from variable.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a single permit leaves unexamined
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unmonitored pathway leaves residents unassisted
questions.stem: A quarry file records that a permit for a quarry covers discharge to water but says nothing about the dust leaving the site. Explain why that gap matters for local residents.

answer.exemplar: Dust from crushing, screening and vehicle movements can carry respirable particles that reach people in nearby homes and on footpaths, and the permit's silence leaves those emissions unmonitored and unlimited. Residents affected by dust have no measured baseline, no trigger level and no way to show a change over time, because the only official figure concerns water they may never use. Advice on exposure therefore has to rest on complaint patterns and indirect measures rather than on the permitted limit, and the note should say that plainly.

questions.explanation: Without a dust limit or monitoring, residents have no baseline, no trigger and no way to evidence change. Advice has to rest on complaints and indirect measures rather than on the permitted figure.
questions.hint: Ask what residents cannot do without a figure.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A denominator that makes the indicator improve
questions.learningObjective: Compute a rate per thousand and interpret a falling rate
questions.stem: A clinic note reports 1,500 appointments completed with 30 complaints, then 2,000 appointments with 30 complaints again. First compute the complaints rate per 1,000 appointments in each period, then state what the change shows.

options.text: The rate falls from 20 to 15 per 1,000 appointments, so a falling rate always means better performance
options.misconception: generalises a falling rate into a quality judgement

options.text: The rate falls from 20 to 15 per 1,000 appointments
The rate rises from 20 to 15 per 1,000 appointments, so service quality deteriorated as volume grew
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the rate change

options.text: The rate is unchanged at 17.5 per 1,000 appointments, because the complaint count did not change
options.misconception: treats an unchanged count as an unchanged rate

questions.explanation: Thirty complaints over 1,500 appointments is 20 per 1,000, and the same 30 over 2,000 is 15 per 1,000. Output grew by a third while the complaint rate fell, which a raw count could never show.
questions.hint: Scale each complaint count to a thousand appointments.
